prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map supports a room-scale layout: across the five frames, the camera turns from the sofa and coffee table on the left/front toward the TV console on the right/front, while the windows and far walls remain roughly 3–6 m away. The sofa and coffee table are generally about 0.5–2 m from the camera wearer, and the TV/console and nearby plants become nearer, roughly 1–2.5 m, in the later frames; the map also separates the foreground furniture from the more distant windows more clearly than RGB alone. No person is reliably visible, so human facing direction, gaze, interpersonal distance, and reach cannot be inferred from this map; furniture entering the brightest foreground regions may be within arm’s reach. The broad depth ordering is plausible, but bright windows, dark regions, object edges, and frame-to-frame scale changes appear unreliable, and some furniture surfaces merge into one smooth depth layer.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map identifies couches, potted plants, a vase, a TV, a laptop, and books, making their identities and visible boundaries clearer than in RGB: couches occupy the left/front in the early frames, while the TV, console objects, and laptop occupy the right/front in the later frames. The coffee-table books and vase appear below and in front of the couch, and the later laptop and book lie beside or below the TV area; nearby objects on the same furniture are likely within roughly 0.2–1 m of one another, although the map itself does not provide metric distance. Across the strip, couch masks move out of view as the camera turns right, while plants and then the TV/laptop enter and enlarge; several masks are clipped at the image borders or partly occluded by furniture. No person is segmented, and depth, facing, gaze, or reach cannot be established reliably; masks are incomplete and inconsistent, with couch and TV regions fragmented or mislabeled and many visible surfaces left black.
descriptions.pose: The pose map contains a sparse yellow skeleton-like detection in the left side of the early view and another near the right side of the final view, but neither aligns convincingly with a visible person in the RGB strip. If interpreted literally, the first detection is low and approximately horizontal near the sofa area, while the last is small, upright, and near the TV/window side; their apparent separation mainly reflects the camera’s turn and does not establish that two people are present or moving. No reliable head orientation, gaze toward the camera wearer, body facing direction, hand position, interpersonal distance, or arm’s-reach relationship can be inferred, and no magenta hand skeleton is clearly present. The map can expose articulated keypoint hypotheses that are hard to notice in RGB, but here it appears highly unreliable because plants, furniture edges, or decorations may have produced false body detections and most expected joints are missing.
